hints: Count the longest continuous carbon chain in acetoin and decide which functional group gives the suffix, the ketone or the alcohol.
walkthrough:
Find the parent chain and main functional group**
Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH(OH)CH}_3$. You have four carbons in a row, so the parent is butane. You have both a ketone ($\text{C=O}$) and an alcohol ($\text{OH}$). Ketone outranks alcohol, so the name ends in -one and the alcohol becomes a hydroxy prefix.

Number to give the ketone the lowest number**
Number from the left so the $\text{C=O}$ is on carbon 2. That puts the $\text{OH}$ on carbon 3. Put it together as 3-hydroxybutan-2-one.

hints: Compare the structures of acetoin and diacetyl and decide what change happens to the $\text{CH(OH)}$ group.
Recall which oxidising agent and heating method converts a secondary alcohol to a ketone without further oxidation.
walkthrough:
Spot the functional group change**
Acetoin has $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH(OH)CH}_3$ and diacetyl has $\text{CH}_3\text{COCOCH}_3$. The $\text{CH(OH)}$ secondary alcohol group has become a $\text{C=O}$ ketone group. That is oxidation, loss of hydrogen.

Choose the standard AS oxidant**
For secondary alcohol to ketone, think acidified dichromate. So warm with $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ in dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. Heating, preferably under reflux, ensures complete oxidation to the diketone.

Final answer: Reagent: acidified potassium dichromate, $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (or $\text{H}^+$ / $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$).
Condition: heat / warm / reflux

hints: Look only at peaks above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and remember that each dip in transmittance corresponds to a bond absorbing IR radiation.
List the bonds present in acetoin, $\text{C=O}$, $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{O-H}$, and think about their typical absorption regions.
Match the broad peak near $3400 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, the sharp peaks near $2900 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and the strong peak near $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ to the correct bonds.
walkthrough:
Read the spectrum correctly**
Remember low transmittance means high absorption. So every deep valley is a bond soaking up IR at that wavenumber. We ignore the messy fingerprint region below $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and focus on the three clear valleys above it.

Assign the carbonyl peak**
See that very strong sharp dip around $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. That is classic for a ketone. In acetoin the $\text{C=O}$ stretch absorbs at 1670 to 1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$.

Assign the C-H and O-H peaks**
The cluster of small sharp dips just below $3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is $\text{C-H}$ stretching, 2850 to 3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. The very broad deep dip centred near $3400 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the hydrogen bonded $\text{O-H}$ stretch, 3200 to 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Broadness is your clue for $\text{O-H}$.

Final answer: Absorption at 1670 to 1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C=O}$.
Absorption at 2850 to 3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C-H}$.
Absorption at 3200 to 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{O-H}$.

hints: Compare the functional groups in acetoin, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH(OH)CH}_3$, with those in diacetyl, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCOCH}_3$.
Decide which absorption present in (c)(i) must disappear when the alcohol group is oxidised to a ketone.
walkthrough:
Focus on what is lost**
Acetoin has an alcohol $\text{OH}$ plus a ketone. Diacetyl has two ketones and no alcohol. So $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-H}$ peaks will still be there, but anything due to $\text{O-H}$ must go.

State the spectral difference**
That means the broad absorption at 3200 to 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ seen for acetoin will be absent for diacetyl. Its absence proves the $\text{O-H}$ group has been oxidised away.

Final answer: No absorption at 3200 to 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ in diacetyl spectrum.
Because diacetyl contains no $\text{O-H}$ bond, the $\text{O-H}$ peak disappears.

hints: Recall what concentrated sulfuric acid does to an alcohol containing a neighbouring $\text{C-H}$ bond.
walkthrough:
Recognise dehydration**
Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a dehydrating agent. It removes $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from an alcohol by elimination. Here $\text{OH}$ leaves from carbon 3 and $\text{H}$ leaves from carbon 4 of $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH(OH)CH}_3$.

Draw the alkene product**
Join carbons 3 and 4 with a double bond while the ketone at carbon 2 is untouched. You get the unsaturated ketone $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH=CH}_2$, but-3-en-2-one.

hints: For cis-trans isomerism, check whether each carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ bond in $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH=CH}_2$ carries two different groups.
For optical isomerism, check whether the product contains a carbon with four different groups attached.
walkthrough:
Test for geometric isomerism**
Picture $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH=CH}_2$. The right hand carbon of the double bond is $\text{CH}_2$, it has two H atoms. Cis-trans isomerism needs two different groups on each $\text{C=C}$ carbon to give distinct arrangements. With two identical H atoms, swapping them gives the same structure, so no geometric isomers.

Test for optical isomerism**
Now look for a chiral centre, a carbon with four different groups. In this product all carbons are either $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C=O}$ or $\text{C=C}$ carbons, none has four single bonds to four different groups. With no chiral centre the molecule is achiral and its mirror image is superimposable, so no enantiomers.

Final answer: No cis-trans / E-Z / geometric isomerism because one $\text{C=C}$ carbon ($\text{CH}_2$) has two identical H atoms attached.
No optical isomerism because there is no chiral carbon, mirror images are superimposable.

hints: Write the product of replacing the $\text{OH}$ in acetoin by Br and examine the carbon bonded to Br.
walkthrough:
See why HBr gives chirality**
HBr substitutes $\text{OH}$ by Br to give $\text{CH}_3\text{COCHBrCH}_3$. Focus on the $\text{CHBr}$ carbon. It is bonded to H, Br, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{COCH}_3$, four completely different groups. That is a chiral or asymmetric carbon, so optical isomerism is possible and a pair of enantiomers forms.
Final answer: Product contains a chiral / asymmetric carbon atom with four different groups attached.

hints: Place the chiral carbon in the centre with its four groups, $\text{COCH}_3$, Br, $\text{CH}_3$ and H, arranged tetrahedrally.
Draw the second structure as the mirror image of the first, swapping the positions of two groups on solid wedge and hashed wedge bonds.
walkthrough:
Set up the first enantiomer**
Draw the central chiral C. Put e.g. $\text{COCH}_3$ at the top, $\text{CH}_3$ at the bottom, Br on a solid wedge coming out towards you and H on a hashed wedge going away. This shows the tetrahedral 3D shape clearly.

Create the mirror image**
For the second enantiomer, keep top and bottom the same but swap left and right, so Br is now on a hashed wedge and H is on a solid wedge, or vice versa. The two drawings should be mirror images that cannot be superimposed, representing the pair of optical isomers of $\text{CH}_3\text{COCHBrCH}_3$.

Final answer: Pair of 3D structures of $\text{CH}_3\text{COC}^*\text{HBrCH}_3$ that are non-superimposable mirror images, with $\text{COCH}_3$, Br, $\text{CH}_3$ and H around the chiral C shown with wedge / dash bonds. One mark for each correct enantiomer.
